newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Bank of China returns.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Bank of China returns.

text.p: Bank of China's long-awaited Hong Kong dollar floating rate certificate of deposit issue will be launched next week, Asian bankers learned Thursday.
Bank of China Group member China Development Finance Co will arrange the five-year HK$2 billion issue, as expected.
CDFC director Barry Mok said the issue has not been fully underwritten. He said this should not be a problem, however, because the syndication is expected to go very well.
The certificates will be the first issue from a Chinese bank to be eligible for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Liquidity Adjustment Facility, or discount window.
Eligibility for LAF makes an issue more attractive to banks because holders of the qualifying debt can engage in repurchase agreements with the monetary authority, increasing liquidity.
The issue is expected to be snapped up by bankers robbed of the chance to own the prestigious paper last year.
Last April, Bank of China yanked a HK$5.0 billion deal after Moody's Investors Service downgraded its rating to Baa1, which made the issue ineligible for LAF.
At that time, eligibility for LAF required that issues must be HK$1.0 billion or more in size and carry ratings of A2 and Single-A by Moody's and Standard and Poor's Corp, respectively.
But in May 1996, the HKMA said that it would accept ratings of the Japan Bond Research Institute (JBRI) and IBCA.
The change meant that many more issuers, notably Bank of China, would be eligible for LAF status.
Last year's suspended Bank of China issue was hugely oversubscribed--it launched at HK$1.0 billion--and bankers said a new issue is likely to be similarly well received.
At the time, bankers said they would have been willing to take the paper, even without LAF status, because of the prestige of the issuer.

Andrew Fung, head of capital markets at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, added that the timing is right for the FRCD. With new issuance of HK$ FRCDs and jumbo loans slack, the Bank of China deal faces little competition.
"The second half of the year has been very quiet so most of the banks should have a lot of room to lend and the market will be extremely liquid," said Fung.
The deal is expected to pay an all-in return of about 40 basis points over the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate.

Such pricing would put the Bank of China deal in line with Standard Chartered Bank's five-year FRCD set in July, which paid that rate to co-lead managers. Bank of China, Standard Chartered Bank and HongKong Bank are the territory's note issuing banks.
In other news, Thailand's Government Housing Bank launched a US$200 million floating rate note issue during early London hours today via lead manager Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The five-year notes pay a coupon of LIBOR flat and were priced to yield LIBOR plus eight basis points.
Fees are 15 basis points.
The issue is fully guaranteed by the Kingdom of Thailand, which is rated Single-A by S&P and A2 by Moody's.
The note is a replacement issue for a Kingdom of Thailand sovereign issue that was mandated to Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in June. The issue would have been Thailand's first Euro-FRN.
Bankers said Thailand had planned to onlend proceeds of the issue to Government Housing Bank.
But they said Thai officials now are encouraging government entities to borrow in international markets in their own names rather than through the central government.
Korea Long-Term Credit Bank launched its A$125 million one year and one day Eurobond via HSBC Markets.
